title: Fresh Pepper Sauce
localName: Fresh pepper sauce — the Ghanaian answer to salsa
author: Barbara Baeta
desc: Crushed in an asanka with a rocking motion for ten or fifteen minutes — because texture is very important in Ghanaian cuisine.
longDesc: This is the raw pepper sauce that sits beside kenkey and fried fish, and the reason it is made in an asanka rather than a blender is stated plainly by its teacher: texture is very important in Ghanaian cuisine. A large onion, a little over eight ounces of plum tomatoes — about a cup and a half chopped — about two tablespoons of minced chili peppers and a teaspoon of salt are crushed in the earthenware bowl with a rocking motion for ten or fifteen minutes. It can optionally be simmered twenty to thirty minutes. Taught by Barbara Baeta.
ingredients: Plum tomatoes — a little over 8 oz, or about 1 1/2 cups chopped
Chili peppers, about 2 tbsp minced, adjust to taste
Salt, about 1 tsp or to taste
equipment: Asanka (earthenware grinding bowl) and wooden grinder
steps: Chop the onion, tomatoes and chillies roughly.
Put them in the asanka with the salt.
Crush with a rocking motion for about 10 or 15 minutes.
// Optional: simmer the finished sauce about 20 to 30 minutes.
Refrigerate and use within a day or so.
chefTips: The rocking motion in the asanka is the technique, for ten or fifteen minutes. Her teacher's reason is the whole point: texture is very important in Ghanaian cuisine, and a blender gives you a smooth purée instead of a crushed sauce.
Ten or fifteen minutes is a long time to crush by hand and it is not negotiable if you want the texture.
The simmer is optional. Raw is fresher and sharper; simmered keeps longer and tastes rounder.
Use within a day or so — her own instruction. This is a fresh sauce and it does not keep like shito.
Two tablespoons of minced chilli for a cup and a half of tomato is a good starting ratio, and it is adjustable.
She calls it the Ghanaian answer to salsa, which is the most useful single description of it.
If you have no asanka, a mortar and pestle is closer than a blender. Pulse a food processor at most.
commonMistakes: Crushing for two minutes instead of ten or fifteen.
Making a large batch — it does not keep.
Simmering it when you wanted the fresh version.
Skipping the salt, which draws the juice out as you crush.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #60: Fresh pepper sauces', betumiblog.blogspot.com, timestamped 2011-06-23. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 5:27 PM'. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 'Salt (about 1 teaspoon or to taste)'; '1 large onion'; plum tomatoes 'a little over 8 oz, or about 1 1/2 cups when chopped'; chili peppers 'about 2 Tablespoons (adjust to taste), minced'.
Method as printed: crush in an asanka with a rocking motion for 'about 10 or 15 minutes'; optional simmer 'about 20-30 minutes'; refrigerate and 'use within a day or so'.

THE REASON FOR THE ASANKA, verbatim, and one of the most useful sentences in this whole collection: 'texture is very important in Ghanaian cuisine'. She also describes the sauce as 'the Ghanaian answer to salsa'.

TAUGHT BY BARBARA BAETA, SINGLE-PASS. Baeta is the Ghanaian chef who co-authored The Ghana Cookbook and runs Flair Catering in Accra; the display author field credits her as the source of the method, with the transcription Osseo-Asare's. This is the second recipe in this collection traceable to Baeta's teaching — the other is ayikple at GHA046 — and almost nothing else attributable to her is retrievable in print.
NO DONENESS CUE beyond the crushing time and the optional simmer. The sauce is raw, so there is nothing to be done.
NO YIELD is printed. The eight servings above is an editorial reading of a cup and a half of tomato.
THE PLURAL TITLE — 'Fresh pepper sauces' — suggests the post covered more than one sauce. Only this one's quantities were obtained.
This sauce is one of the accompaniments named in the Ga kenkey post at GHA037, where she lists 'a fresh hot pepper sauce' alongside shito and fried fish, and cross-refers to this recipe number.
storage: A day or so refrigerated, per the author. The simmered version keeps a few days longer.
reheating: Not needed. Served cold or at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Raw, so it keeps the full vitamin C of the tomatoes and chillies.
Very low in calories with no added oil.
Onion and chilli both carry documented bioactive compounds.
culturalNote: An asanka is a ribbed earthenware bowl and food crushed in one comes out quite unlike anything a blade produces — uneven, juicy, with recognisable pieces. That a professional Accra caterer taught this sauce with an insistence on the vessel, rather than the ingredients, says most of what needs saying about Ghanaian cooking.
